Democrats did not “break” the health care system. Before the Affordable Care Act, insurers could deny coverage for preexisting conditions, drop people when they got sick, impose lifetime caps, and price millions out of the market entirely. The ACA reduced the uninsured rate to historic lows, expanded Medicaid, capped out of pocket costs for seniors, and later Democratic legislation allowed Medicare to negotiate drug prices for the first time. That is the opposite of a broken system, even though the system still has cost problems that require real solutions.

The “Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act” does not lower underlying health care costs. What it does is reduce federal spending by cutting ACA subsidies, weakening Medicaid protections, and shifting costs onto states, employers, and patients. Independent analyses of similar House Republican proposals show premiums do not fall for most people, especially older Americans and those with chronic conditions. Coverage becomes skimpier, deductibles rise, and more people are uninsured. Lower federal spending is not the same thing as lower health care costs for families.

The claim that the bill “expands choices” is also a lie. Allowing cheaper plans with fewer benefits and weaker consumer protections increases choice on paper while exposing people to higher out of pocket costs when they actually need care. This is exactly what happened before the ACA, when so called choice meant junk plans that failed people when they got sick. Choice without adequate coverage is not affordability.

The statement about reducing prescription drug costs is flatly contradicted by Republican voting records. House Republicans overwhelmingly opposed allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices and opposed caps on insulin and other out of pocket drug costs. The only legislation that has actually reduced prescription drug prices came from Democrats, not Republicans. This bill does not give Medicare new negotiating power or impose price limits on drug companies.

The graphic promises lower costs, more affordability, and cheaper drugs, but the legislation does none of that. It reduces coverage, weakens protections, and shifts costs onto Americans while preserving higher prices for insurers and drug companies. That is why the claims in the post are lies.
